Memory.value: I can't seem to put the frightening event into words.
Sometimes I can recall what happened but feel completely numb, as if it happened to a stranger
My memories of the event come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together

vignette:
Ethan Walker is a 29-year-old Coast Guard serviceman who came to treatment after months of feeling unsettled by a robbery he still struggled to describe in any ordinary way. He had been mugged late one evening after stopping at a convenience store on his way home. The night itself remained strangely hard for him to tell straight through. He could give the bare outline: the parking lot, a man approaching too fast, a weapon glimpsed at close range, the demand for his wallet and phone. But when he tried to say more, his speech would stall. He would gesture with his hands, fall silent, and then say that what happened did not come back to him as a story so much as flashes-light off the asphalt, the man's sleeve, the shape of his own keys in his palm, the sound of his breathing suddenly turning loud in his ears. He said he "couldn't put it into words right," and this difficulty was not evasiveness so much as a genuine sense that the worst part of it existed outside language.

In the first days afterward, Ethan told his girlfriend and a police officer what he could remember, but even then the account felt broken apart. One moment in his memory was standing by his car; another was staring at the ground; then another was being aware that the man had already run off. What came between those moments felt missing or scrambled. He was troubled by how little continuity there seemed to be. He knew he had been terrified, yet when he tried to revisit the event later, he would sometimes find himself recounting it in a flat, detached way, as if he were talking about surveillance footage of someone else. He noticed this especially when people asked practical questions-what the man looked like, what was taken, whether he had thought he would be killed. Ethan would hear himself answer, calm and almost mechanical, and the absence of feeling was unnerving in its own right. At other times he would stop mid-sentence because all he had were disconnected pieces that would not join.

The robbery happened off base, but its presence followed him into his daily life in a way that felt jarring. In the Coast Guard, Ethan was used to reading situations quickly, staying alert, and functioning under pressure. Since the mugging, however, ordinary moments around parking lots, dim building entrances, and isolated stretches near gas stations had begun to feel charged in a way he could not easily explain to others. Walking from his car for an early shift, he might catch sight of a stranger moving in his peripheral vision and be abruptly pulled into one of those sensory fragments from the night of the robbery-the angle of someone closing distance, the hard brightness of lot lights, the sense of his body bracing before his mind had caught up. Because the memory arrived in pieces rather than as a coherent recollection, he often felt wrong-footed by it. There was no beginning, middle, and end he could hold onto, only bursts of image and bodily knowing.

Over the following months, this altered how he moved through his days. He started choosing routes and errands based on whether they would require him to stop alone at night. If he needed to pick something up after work, he would ask his girlfriend to come with him or put it off entirely. He lingered before getting out of his car, scanning the area in a way that felt sensible to him given what had happened. On base, he preferred staying close to others when crossing lot areas after dark. None of this looked dramatic from the outside, but it narrowed his world. His girlfriend noticed that simple tasks had become negotiations, and Ethan, who had always thought of himself as capable and steady, found it hard to explain why something as small as a convenience store stop now felt loaded.

What unsettled him most was not only the robbery itself, but the way his mind seemed to hold it. He could not make the memory line up into a complete account, and when it did come back, he often felt nothing at all for a few moments, which left him doubting his own reactions. Then a fragment would surface unexpectedly and he would feel caught off guard by how immediate it seemed. He had begun to worry that if he could not say what happened properly, he did not really have command of it.

By the time he sought help, Ethan was worn down by the strangeness of living beside an event that felt both vivid and inaccessible. He came in at his girlfriend's urging after another stalled attempt to explain the robbery ended with him staring at the floor, able to name only scattered details. He said he wanted to be able to tell the story "like a normal memory" instead of feeling ambushed by pieces of it. What he feared most was that this fractured, numb, wordless quality would stay with him indefinitely; what he hoped for was something simple and specific-to be able to walk through his life, including the parking lots and nighttime routines his job required, without feeling as though one unfinished moment were waiting there for him.
